sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Initial Sepsis Management
sections.description: This section details the initial patient presentation following the dog bite, focusing on the rapid progression to septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). It covers the epidemiology of Capnocytophaga canimorsus, the clinical signs of fulminant sepsis, and the immediate stabilization measures required before the underlying thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) becomes apparent.
subtopics: Epidemiology and transmission risks of Capnocytophaga canimorsus in dog bite victims
Clinical features of fulminant sepsis: hypoglycemia, pancytopenia, and mottled extremities
Differentiating early sepsis-induced DIC from primary thrombotic microangiopathy
Initial empiric antibiotic selection and supportive care in septic shock
Recognition of warning signs for progression to multiorgan failure

sections.description: This section explains the biological mechanisms linking bacterial infection to complement-mediated haemolytic uraemic syndrome (CM-HUS). It focuses on the dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, the specific interaction between C. canimorsus and host immunity, and how infection acts as a 'second hit' in susceptible individuals.
subtopics: Overview of the complement system and the alternative pathway
Mechanisms of endothelial damage and thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA)
C. canimorsus virulence factors and complement evasion strategies
The concept of infection as a trigger for complement dysregulation
Genetic predisposition versus acquired complement activation in CM-HUS

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning and Differential Diagnosis of TMA
sections.description: This section guides the reader through the complex diagnostic workup required to distinguish CM-HUS from other causes of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA). It emphasizes the exclusion of TTP and STEC-HUS, the interpretation of laboratory markers, and the utility of renal biopsy in confirming the diagnosis.
subtopics: The TMA triad: MAHA, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury (AKI)
Excluding Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) using ADAMTS13 activity and PLASMIC score
Ruling out Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC-HUS) via stool PCR
Interpreting complement levels (C3/C4) and functional assays in active disease
Role of renal biopsy in confirming TMA and excluding glomerulonephritis

sections.section_title: Therapeutic Strategies and Management of CM-HUS
sections.description: This section outlines the therapeutic decision-making process for CM-HUS, particularly in the context of active infection. It compares plasma exchange (PEX) with complement inhibition, discusses the risks of eculizumab during bacteraemia, and details the necessary prophylactic measures.
subtopics: Indications and limitations of plasma exchange (PEX) in CM-HUS
Mechanism of action and timing of eculizumab therapy
Managing the risk of encapsulated bacterial infection during complement blockade
Vaccination protocols (meningococcal) and antibiotic prophylaxis requirements
Criteria for transitioning from induction to maintenance therapy

sections.section_title: Clinical Outcome, Prognosis, and Educational Implications
sections.description: This section reviews the patient's long-term recovery, the factors influencing renal prognosis, and the broader clinical lessons derived from this case. It highlights the importance of early recognition and the growing recognition of rare infectious triggers for CM-HUS.
subtopics: Trajectory of renal recovery and long-term dialysis dependence risks
Monitoring for disease relapse and duration of complement blockade
Prognostic factors: time to eculizumab initiation and baseline renal function
Importance of considering rare zoonotic infections in TMA workups
Key takeaways for clinicians managing sepsis-associated TMA
